# Notes for the House-Sitter

Thank you again for doing this on such short notice. I know two weeks is a long time, and I know Priya told you it was "basically just a dog," which is true, but there are a few things.

**1. The dog.** His name is Biscuit. He will tell you he hasn't been fed. He has been fed. He eats one scoop in the morning and one at night, and the scoop is the red one, not the blue one, because the blue one is bigger and he knows it. If you use the blue one he will look at you with enormous gratitude and then throw up on the stairs around 2 a.m.

He is not technically my dog. I'll explain that further down, or I won't. Either way, feed him.

**2. The front door** sticks in humid weather. Lift the handle up while you turn the key. There's a knack. You'll get it by the second day. It took me four years, but I was married to someone who always got to the door first, so I never had to learn.

**3. The thermostat** is set to 68. Please leave it at 68. There is a sticky note on it that says "DON'T TOUCH – M." You can ignore the M part. The M part is not relevant anymore. But leave it at 68 anyway, because I've gotten used to it, which is its own kind of problem.

**4. The plants.** The fern in the kitchen needs water every other day. The snake plant in the living room needs water approximately never. You could leave for a year and come back and it would still be there, looking at you, faintly disappointed. I admire it very much.

There is a third plant on the upstairs landing. It is dead. Please don't water it, and please don't throw it out. I know how that sounds.

**5. Trash** goes out Tuesday night. Recycling is every other Tuesday, and I have never once known which Tuesday. I usually just look at what the neighbors do. The Hendersons on the left are reliable. The man on the right puts his bins out on random days, possibly as a form of protest. Follow the Hendersons.

**6. Mail.** Just stack it on the counter. If anything comes addressed to Michael Okafor, please put it in the shoebox by the door. He's coming by to pick it up at some point. He has a key. He may also take the dog for an afternoon; that's fine; that's arranged. If he comes, he'll probably be polite and a little too friendly, and he may ask how I'm doing. You don't have to answer. You can say you don't know me that well, which is true, and which will be a relief to both of you.

**7. The upstairs room at the end of the hall.** You don't need to go in there. It's not locked or anything. It's not a Bluebeard situation. It's just that it was going to be something, and then it wasn't, and there's still a can of paint in there in a color called "Morning Oat," which I picked because I thought it was a funny name, and he picked because he thought I would like it, and it turns out we both just wanted the other person to be happy with the paint. That's not nothing. I think about that more than I think about the other stuff.

Anyway, the Wi-Fi router is in there, so if the internet goes out you'll have to go in and unplug it and plug it back in. Sorry.

**8. Wi-Fi password** is on the fridge. Don't judge it. It was chosen in a different era.

**9. Biscuit, continued.** He sleeps at the foot of the bed, on the left side. If you're in the guest room, he will cry at the door for about ten minutes and then give up and sleep in the hallway. If you want to let him in, let him in. For the first month after Michael left, Biscuit slept by the front door every night, waiting, and I didn't know how to explain to him that the thing he was waiting for was not going to happen in the way he wanted. Then one night he came upstairs and got on the bed on the left side, where he'd never been allowed, and I didn't stop him. So now that's where he goes.

We decided he'd stay here because the house has a yard and Michael's new apartment doesn't. That was the reason we said out loud. I think the real reason is that Michael knew I would need something to feed twice a day. He was always good at knowing what I needed, just not at being it. Those turn out to be different skills.

**10. Where I'll be.** I'm going to my sister's, on the coast. She says I need to "get out of the house," as if the house were the problem. The house is fine. The house is great, actually. The door sticks and the Tuesdays are a mystery, but it holds up.

My number is on the fridge, under the Wi-Fi password. Call if anything catches fire, including metaphorically.

**11. One last thing.** The dead plant on the landing was the first thing we bought together, the week we moved in. A little lemon tree. We had big ideas about lemonade. It never fruited, not once, and in March it just quietly stopped. I haven't been able to throw it out. I think I'm waiting until throwing it out means something smaller.

If, while I'm gone, you look at it and think, *that's just a dead plant in a pot*, then maybe you're right. Maybe when I get back, I'll see it that way too.

But leave it for now.

Help yourself to anything in the fridge. The good coffee is in the freezer. Biscuit will try to convince you otherwise, but he's already eaten.

Thank you. Really.

— D.

Actually I like a form-driven idea better—a story told as numbered instructions left for a house-sitter that gradually reveal the homeowner's divorce, with the husband gone, the dog being his, an empty upstairs room. I'll title it "Notes for the House-Sitter," keep it darkly funny but tender, and aim for around 1000 words.
